text: The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight contains all colors of the visible spectrum, and when it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with tiny gas molecules—mainly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light (blue and violet) much more strongly than longer wavelengths (red and orange)—in fact, blue light is scattered roughly four times more than red light. This scattered blue light spreads across the sky in all directions, so wherever you look, you see blue. The sky isn't violet instead, even though violet is scattered even more, because the sun emits less violet light and our eyes are less sensitive to it. This also explains why sunsets look red and orange: when the sun is low, its light travels through more atmosphere, so the blue light is scattered away before reaching your eyes, leaving the longer wavelengths behind.
